content: Patients with mutations in either the inhA promoter region or the katG gene were included in the study. These mutations are associated with resistance to isoniazid, a key anti-tuberculosis drug. Resistance levels vary depending on the mutation: inhA mutations alone confer low-level resistance, while katG mutations alone or in combination with inhA mutations result in high-level resistance. Additionally, inhA promoter mutations are linked to resistance against ethionamide and prothionamide. When both inhA and katG mutations are present, high-dose isoniazid and thioamides are ineffective, making the 9-month treatment regimen unsuitable for such cases. In the absence of individual mutation data, decisions can be guided by drug-resistance surveillance data on the frequency of concurrent mutations. Testing for resistance to ethambutol and ethionamide is considered unreliable and should be interpreted cautiously when informing treatment regimens. Globally, there is limited capacity for drug susceptibility testing (DST) for bedaquiline, but laboratory infrastructure must be strengthened as new drugs and regimens are increasingly adopted. National and reference laboratories need access to appropriate reagents and data on the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) distribution of circulating Mycobacterium tuberculosis lineages. The WHO TB Supranational Reference Laboratory Network supports national TB reference laboratories in conducting quality-assured DST. In 2017, the WHO established critical concentrations for susceptibility testing of fluoroquinolones, bedaquiline, delamanid, clofazimine, and linezolid. The choice of fluoroquinolones, such as levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, is influenced by their efficacy and safety profiles. Both drugs have shown similar effectiveness in treating drug-resistant TB (DR-TB). However, moxifloxacin carries a slightly higher risk of cardiotoxicity, while levofloxacin has been associated with musculoskeletal disorders in pediatric populations. Levofloxacin is often preferred in all-oral regimens, while moxifloxacin may be used in shorter regimens with injectables. Regardless of the choice, national TB programs must implement drug safety monitoring (DSM) for all patients undergoing DR-TB treatment. Chest radiography plays a critical role in assessing the extent of TB disease, particularly in identifying bilateral cavitary disease or extensive parenchymal damage. In children under 15 years, advanced disease is typically defined by the presence of cavities or bilateral disease on chest radiographs. This highlights the importance of radiographic evaluation in diagnostic and clinical management. The recommended 9-month regimen for DR-TB includes an intensive phase of 4 months, extendable to 6 months, followed by a continuation phase of 5 months, resulting in a total duration of up to 11 months. In the reviewed dataset, bedaquiline and linezolid were used for 6 and 2 months, respectively. Patient-centered approaches are essential to ensure adherence to treatment, and active monitoring of adverse events is critical for safety and effectiveness. The WHO emphasizes the need for routine DST not only for patient selection but also for monitoring the emergence of drug resistance. Reliable DST for bedaquiline and linezolid is particularly important when bacteriological conversion is not observed by the end of the fourth month of treatment. Pediatric formulations and their sustained availability are crucial for implementing shorter regimens in children. Further research priorities include evaluating shorter regimens (<6 months) with bedaquiline, comparing the effectiveness of these regimens in specific populations (e.g., children, pregnant women, patients with extrapulmonary TB), and understanding the mechanisms of bedaquiline resistance. Identifying optimal companion drugs to protect bedaquiline and limit resistance acquisition is also a key area of focus. The COVID-19 pandemic has significantly disrupted TB services, leading to a decline in TB diagnoses and an increase in TB-related deaths. Access to treatment for drug-resistant TB has also decreased, with a 15% drop in enrollment for MDR/RR-TB treatment between 2019 and 2020. Despite these challenges, treatment success rates for MDR/RR-TB have improved globally, reaching 59% in 2018. However, the need for shorter, safer, and more effective regimens remains critical to optimize outcomes and reduce the burden of drug-resistant TB.
